nodes.label: Strategy
nodes.question: What is GI generally considered as in the context of stormwater management?
nodes.answer: GI is generally considered an alternative engineering approach for stormwater management that also includes temperature control and air quality management.
nodes.paragraph: GI is generally considered an alternative engineering approach for stormwater management that also includes temperature control and air quality management. The terms Nature- Based Solutions, green-grey infrastructure, sustainable urban drainage systems, ecologi- cal infrastructure and sponge cities have been widely used in GI debates across the years based on specific objectives (Alves et al., 2024; Seidu et al., 2024; Yuan et al., 2024). These new directions are integrated systems that are designed to perform multitudes of functionality in a manner analogous to that of natural processes. Consequentially, GI systems have the potential to become an essential tool in the management of excessive rainfall in urban regions. Proponents of GI have perused the concept from diverse applications, disciplines and multifunctional dimensions (Alves et al., 2024). The question of what drives GI adop- tion and implementation success is therefore based on the region, stakeholders percep- tions and knowledge levels. Engineers and built environment professionals may convey and recommend GI to clients based on their own understanding of what GI is due to the multifunctional nature of these systems. Some key attributional drivers include com- munity well-being enhancement, urban heat island mitigation, environmental sustain- ability, ecosystem services provision and biodiversity enhancement.

nodes.question: What are some criteria identified for selecting best management practices in stormwater management?
nodes.answer: The criteria for selecting best management practices in stormwater management involve addressing the conflicting preferences of stakeholders.
nodes.paragraph: Among these applications, it is possible to highlight the use of MCA to compare and select green and gray infrastructure for flood risk reduction and management, considering also environmental and social co-benefits [ 19 21], to integrate 1 3 Circular Economy and Sustainabilitystakeholders preferences into planning of NBS for managing hydro-meteorological risks at the river basin scale [ 19], and to select best management practices in stormwater best management practices involving conflicting stakeholders [ 22]. Bousquet et al. (2023) [ 23], present a comprehensive review of MCA applications in NBS planning and among 124 reviewed papers they evidence the lack of stakeholders involvement in the MCA process through participatory workshops. From the selected papers, none refer to the involvement of municipal or citizen representatives, nor do they incorporate private sector professionals. Land management research has widely explored the incorporation of MCA methods, either with combination with Geo-tools, such as GIS [ 24, 25], or in the form of Spatial MCA [ 26, 27], allowing the incorporation of criteria related to biodiversity, ecosystem services or resilience for identification of best strategies to implement ecosystem restoration or urban greening practices.
